new_entities.name: Long working hours
new_entities.description: Occupational exposure to persistently long work schedules or high overtime hours.

edges.effect_quant: The broad pooled literature leans toward higher stroke risk with very long work hours, but later cohort evidence suggests the signal may depend on stroke subtype rather than showing a uniform increase in overall stroke.
edges.population: working-age adults exposed to extended weekly work hours
edges.mechanism: Long hours can increase stress load, reduce sleep, and worsen blood-pressure and recovery patterns, which offers a plausible vascular pathway to stroke. The weaker overall epidemiology suggests that any effect may be strongest for haemorrhagic events or in more susceptible subgroups.
edges.summary: This is not a slam-dunk edge, but it is more than noise. The WHO/ILO stroke meta-analysis supports a harmful association with long working hours, whereas the Danish workforce cohort did not replicate a higher overall stroke rate and instead hinted at a subtype-specific signal for haemorrhagic stroke.
edges.caveats: Stroke subtype matters here, and the observational literature mixes different hour thresholds, occupations, and confounder adjustments. The right reading is modest and somewhat heterogeneous harm, not a universally large effect.

evidence.citation: Descatha Alexandre et al 2020 Environ Int
evidence.notes: The effect of exposure to long working hours on stroke: A systematic review and meta-analysis from the WHO/ILO Joint Estimates of the Work-related Burden of Disease and Injury.
